meta.title: Descope ad teardown: six pillars promised, none of them named
meta.meta_desc: A teardown of Descope’s LinkedIn ad: a real enterprise pain and a page that matches it, but neither ever names the six pillars, and a gated checklist runs with no proof.
meta.og_desc: Six pillars promised. None of them named.

voice.lede: Descope picked a pain every engineering lead selling upmarket has lived: enterprise deals stall when identity gaps show up late. The ad and the page match almost word for word, which is rarer than it should be. The gap is what both of them hold back. Six pillars are promised twice and never named, and a gated checklist asks for four fields with no logo, number or customer beside the form.

findings.title: A pain the buyer has already lived
findings.what: “Enterprise deals stall when identity gaps surface too late” names a specific, expensive moment. A VP of Engineering recognizes it instantly, with no jargon in the way.

findings.title: Six pillars, none of them named
findings.what: The copy promises a score across “six foundational pillars” and stops there. SSO, SCIM and delegated admin are what the buyer is worried about, and the ad never says them.
findings.fix: Name two or three pillars in the ad. Specifics are what make a checklist feel worth a work email.

findings.title: No proof on the creative
findings.what: The creative is a staircase of checkmarks leading to a bank icon. It is clean and on-topic, and it carries no customer logo or number.
findings.fix: Add one customer logo or a line on who has already passed the checklist.

findings.title: The promise survives the click
findings.what: The ad and the page use the same title, the same six-pillar frame and the same asset. Nobody lands wondering if they are in the right place.

findings.title: The headline names the asset, not the payoff
findings.what: “A Practical Checklist for B2B Enterprise Readiness” describes the document. It leaves out what the reader walks away able to do.
findings.fix: Lead with the outcome: know which identity gaps will stall your next enterprise deal.

findings.title: A gated asset with zero proof
findings.what: Four fields stand next to three bullets, with no logos, no download count and no preview of what is inside. For a gated asset, this is where confidence drops.
findings.fix: Put three or four customer logos beside the form and show one page of the checklist.

faq.q: What is wrong with Descope’s LinkedIn ad?
faq.a: The pain is right and the match is tight. The ad’s weakness is what it withholds: six pillars are promised and never named, and the creative carries no proof.

faq.q: Why does naming the pillars matter?
faq.a: Pillars are what the reader is trading a work email for. Naming SSO, SCIM or delegated admin tells them the checklist covers their real problem, and it pre-qualifies the click.

faq.q: How should a gated checklist page build trust?
faq.a: Put proof next to the form: customer logos, a download count or a preview page. The form is the moment of doubt, so that is where the evidence belongs.

issues.title: Headline Clarity
issues.explanation: "Enterprise deals stall when identity gaps surface too late" names a real, specific pain that VPs of Eng recognize instantly. Clear, no jargon soup.

issues.title: CTA Friction
issues.explanation: This is a content offer (checklist download), not a demo ask, so low friction is appropriate. No written CTA line in the ad copy itself is a minor gap.

issues.title: Visual-Copy Match
issues.explanation: Creative shows a rising staircase of checkmarks toward a bank icon, matching "score your readiness across six pillars." Clean but generic stock-style icon work.

issues.title: Benefit Specificity
issues.explanation: "Six foundational pillars" is repeated everywhere but never named in the ad or creative. What are they? SSO, SCIM, MFA? Say it.

issues.title: Trust Signals
issues.explanation: No customer logos or proof points on the creative image itself. LinkedIn supports logo badges here and this ad skips that lever entirely.
